definitions.text: Kine. [Scot.] See Kee, Kie, and Kine.
A pack sack to be swung on either side of a packsaddle. [Western U. S.]
See Cyanite.
To render (wood) proof against decay by saturating with a solution of corrosive sublimate in open tanks, or under pressure.
Same as Cyanophyll.
Cocoanut fiber, or the cordage made from it. See Coir.
A daw. [Scot.]
p. p. of Kythe.
imp. of Kythe, to show. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To look steadfastly; to gaze. [Obs.] [Written also kike, keke.] This Nicholas sat ever gaping upright, As he had kyked on the newe moon. Chaucer.
A variety of the boomerang.
The cattle of the Hebrides, or of the Highlands. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.
See Kimnel. [Obs.] Chapman.
An instrument for measuring, and recording graphically, the pressure of the blood in any of the blood vessels of a living animal;
Of or pertaining to a kymograph; as, a kymographic tracing.
See Cymric, a. & n.
See Cymry.
Kindred. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Pertaining to, or designating, an acid obtained from the urine of dogs. By decomposition the acid yields a nitrogenous base (called kynurin) and carbonic acid. [Written also cynurenic.]
See Kyrie eleison.
(R. C. Ch.)
Greek words, meaning "Lord, have mercy upon us," used in the Mass, the breviary offices, the litany of the saints, etc. Addis & Arnold.
The name given to the response to the Commandments, in the service of the Church of England and of the Protestant Episcopal Church.
A litany beginning with the words. "Kyrie eleison." Shipley.
The use of literal or simple expressions, as distinguished from the use of figurative or obscure ones. Krauth-Fleming.
The use of literal or simple expressions, as distinguished from the use of figurative or obscure ones. Krauth-Fleming.

Serving to denote objects by conventional signs or alphabetical characters; as, the original Greek alphabet of sixteen letters was called kyriologic, because it represented the pure elementary sounds. See Curiologic. [Written also curiologic and kuriologic.] hieroglyphics, in which a part is put conventionally for the whole, as in depicting a battle by two hands, one holding a shield and the other a bow.
To make known; to manifest; to show; to declare. [Obs: or Scot.] For gentle hearte kytheth gentilesse. Chaucer.
To come into view; to appear. [Scot.] It kythes bright . . . because all is dark around it. Sir W. Scott.
See Karyomiton.
See Karyoplasma.
